idiom_name: abstract base class with pure virtual members + virtual destructor
implementation_notes: C++ expresses the layer supertype directly: an abstract base class declares pure virtual members (= 0) for what each layer member must supply and concrete, ideally final, members for the behavior and state the layer shares, while a virtual destructor makes deletion through a base pointer well defined. Pointers and references to the abstract type give uniform runtime treatment, which is why the virtual base remains the default realization even though CRTP can supply the same shared code with static dispatch. CRTP - a template <class Derived> base calling static_cast<Derived*>(this) - removes the vtable and enables inlining, but each instantiation is a distinct type, so reserve it for shared behavior that does not need one runtime type for the layer.
pitfalls: A base class without a virtual destructor makes deleting a derived object through a base pointer undefined behaviour.
Calling a virtual member from the base constructor or destructor binds to the base version, because the derived part does not exist yet - the classic half-initialised layer object.
Slicing: passing a layer object by value to a parameter of base type copies only the base subobject; layer APIs must take references or pointers.

variants.name: CRTP static base (compile-time polymorphism)
variants.implementation_notes: The layer's base is a template: template <class Derived> struct LayerBase implements the shared behavior in terms of static_cast<Derived*>(this), so the code is instantiated into each member, inlined, and no vtable is emitted. The cost is that the layer has no single runtime type - LayerBase<A> and LayerBase<B> are unrelated - so use CRTP for shared implementation that never needs uniform runtime treatment, and keep the abstract virtual base when layer objects must be stored or passed through one type.
pitfalls: No common runtime type: the 'one declared type per layer' promise becomes compile-time only, so mixed collections need the virtual base or type erasure.
static_cast to a type that does not actually derive from the base is undefined behaviour, and mistakes surface as confusing downstream template diagnostics.
Every instantiation duplicates the base's code, growing binary size where the virtual version shares one implementation.
